title: The Interview
blurb: The job you need is one interview away — at two o'clock today. But the trains are down, a document is missing, and a smooth stranger is offering an easy way to fake your way in. With the clock running and someone from your past on the panel, you have one morning to get there as yourself — and earn it honestly.

identity.name: Interview at Two
identity.mood: A cold morning, a warm chance: the interview that could change everything is at two, and the city is against you.

cover.alt: A warm-lit interview-room window high in a cool glass tower at dusk, rain on the street below, one warm window among the cold ones.

line.en: The interview that could change everything is at two o'clock, and the morning is already against you. Get there, as yourself, and earn it straight.
line.fr: L'entretien qui peut tout changer est à quatorze heures, et la matinée est déjà contre toi. Arrives-y en restant toi-même, et mérite-le honnêtement.
line.es: La entrevista que podría cambiarlo todo es a las dos, y la mañana ya está en tu contra. Llega allí siendo tú mismo, y gánatelo con honradez.
line.it: Il colloquio che potrebbe cambiare tutto è alle due, e la mattinata è già contro di te. Arrivaci restando te stesso, e meritatelo con onestà.
line.de: Das Vorstellungsgespräch, das alles verändern könnte, ist um zwei, und der Morgen ist schon gegen dich. Komm hin, bleib du selbst, und verdien es dir ehrlich.
line.pt: A entrevista que pode mudar tudo é às duas, e a manhã já está contra ti. Chega lá sendo tu mesmo, e merece-a com honestidade.
line.ru: Собеседование, которое может изменить всё, — в два часа, а утро уже против тебя. Доберись туда, оставаясь собой, и заслужи это честно.
line.zh: 那场可能改变一切的面试在两点，而这个上午已经处处跟你作对。赶到那里，做你自己，堂堂正正地赢下它。
line.ar: المقابلة التي قد تُغيّر كل شيء في الساعة الثانية، والصباح بالفعل ضدّك. اوصل إلى هناك كما أنت، واستحقّها بنزاهة.

hero.sub: A story where you are the hero — and every choice turns you to a new page. Written for people learning English, at your level, with meaning in your language whenever you need it.

text.A2: It is one o'clock. The interview that could change everything is at two. You have been out of work for months. The rent is late, and your dad is counting on you. But your bag is a mess, one paper is missing, and the trains are down. Getting there is all on you now.
text.B1: It is one o'clock, and the interview that could change everything is at two. You have been out of work for months now. The rent is late, and your dad is counting on you. But your bag is a mess, the one paper you need is missing, and the trains are down. For the first time, getting there is all on you.
text.B2: It is one o'clock, and the interview that could change everything is at two. You have been out of work for months now, and it shows. The rent is late, and your dad — who always said you'd land on your feet — is counting on you. But your bag is a mess, the one paper you really need is missing, and the trains are down across the city. For the first time, getting there, as yourself and on time, is all on you.

text.A2: Take stock of what you have.
text.B1: Take stock of what you have.
text.B2: Take stock of what you have.

text.A2: You look at what you have to work with. Your one good suit, the job advert, a pen, your phone. But the paper with the address and the time is gone. It is already past one, and the clock is loud in your head. You must decide what to do, and move fast.
text.B1: You look at what you have to work with. Your one good suit, the job advert, a pen, your phone. But the paper with the address and the time on it is gone. It's already past one, and the clock is loud in your head. You have to decide what to do, and move fast.
text.B2: You look at what you have to work with. Your one good suit, the printed job advert, a pen that still works, your phone. But the paper with the address and the time on it — the one thing you can't do without — is gone. It's already past one, and the clock is loud in your head. You have to decide what to do, and you have to move fast.

text.A2: You call an old workmate to ask what to do. The phone rings and rings. Then she picks up. She can't meet you — she's miles away. But she talks you through it, calmly. 'Be yourself,' she says. 'You've done the work. You can do this.' And somehow you start to believe her.
text.B1: You call an old workmate to ask what to do. The phone rings and rings, and then at last she picks up. She can't meet you — she's miles away. But she talks you through it, calmly, step by step. 'Be yourself,' she says. 'You've done the work. You can do this.' And somehow you start to believe her.
text.B2: You call an old workmate to ask what on earth to do. The phone rings and rings, and then at last she picks up. She can't meet you today — she's miles away across the country. But she talks you through it anyway, calmly, step by step. 'Be yourself,' she says. 'You've done the work. You can do this.' And somehow, hearing her, you start to believe it.

text.A2: You call home first. Your dad picks up, and his voice steadies you at once. 'You'll be grand,' he says. But the clock is still running, and you are still not ready. Sitting on the phone won't get you there. You need your papers, a plan, and a clear head before you go.
text.B1: You call home first. Your dad picks up, and his voice steadies you at once. 'You'll be grand,' he says. But the clock is still running, and you're still not ready. Sitting on the phone won't get you there. You need your papers, a plan, and a clear head before you go.
text.B2: You call home first, before anything else. Your dad picks up, and his voice steadies you at once. 'You'll be grand,' he says, the way he always does. But the clock is still running, and you're still not ready. Sitting on the phone to him won't get you across the city. You need your papers, a plan, and a clear head before you so much as leave the flat.

text.A2: You pull yourself together and get ready. You press your shirt, check your shoes, and breathe. Outside, the street is grey and wet. Then your phone buzzes — a message from a number you don't know. 'I can help you get that job,' it says. You weren't expecting anything like that.
text.B1: You pull yourself together and get ready to go. You press your shirt, check your shoes, and breathe. Outside, the street is grey and wet. Then your phone buzzes — a message from a number you don't know. 'I can help you get that job,' it says. You weren't expecting anything like that, not today.
text.B2: You pull yourself together and get ready to go. You press your shirt, check your shoes, and try to breathe slowly. Outside, the street is grey and wet and unhelpful. Then your phone buzzes — a message from a number you don't recognise. 'I can help you get that job,' it says, and nothing more. You weren't expecting anything like that, not today of all days.

text.A2: You make yourself stop and think. You could set off right now and sort the rest on the way. You could get your papers in order first. Or you could call round for help and a lift. Each choice costs time you don't have. And the clock keeps moving toward two.
text.B1: You make yourself stop and think. You could set off right now and sort the rest on the way. You could get your papers in order first. Or you could call round for help and a lift. Each choice costs time you don't have — and the clock keeps moving toward two.
text.B2: You make yourself stop and think for a moment. You could set off right now and sort the rest out on the way. You could get all your papers in order first, properly. Or you could call round for help and maybe a lift across town. Each choice costs time you don't have — and the clock keeps moving, steadily, toward two.

text.A2: The time presses on you like a weight. You think of the panel waiting at two, of the late rent, of your dad's quiet hope. A whole new life rests on this one hour. That isn't a worry; it's a plain fact. No one else can walk in there for you. It is you, today, or no one.

text.A2: The print shop is still open. Old Sam waves you in out of the rain. 'Use the machine,' he says. 'Pay me when you can.' He points you to it. Print your CV, your letter, the address, the map. Everything you need to walk in ready. He's a good sort, Sam.
text.B1: The print shop is still open, and old Sam waves you in out of the rain. 'Use the machine,' he says. 'Pay me when you can.' He points you to it. Print your CV, your letter, the address, the map. Everything you need to walk in ready is here. He's a good sort, Sam.
text.B2: The print shop is still open, and old Sam waves you in out of the rain. 'Use the machine,' he says. 'Pay me when you're able.' He points you to it in the corner. Print your CV, your covering letter, the address, the map — everything you need to walk in ready is right here. He's a good sort, Sam, and always has been.

text.A2: Near the station, you see her. A young woman stands frozen at the barrier, her ticket jammed, the crowd pushing past. She can't get through, and no one stops. 'Can you help?' she asks. You've an interview to reach and no time. But she's right here, stuck, and asking you.

text.B2: Near the station, you see her. A young woman stands frozen at the ticket barrier, her ticket jammed, the crowd pushing past on both sides. She can't get through, and no one stops for her. text.A2: You just set off, fast and half-ready. You grab your bag and go. But you've no real plan, and half your papers are loose in your hand. Rushing like this, it won't come together on its own. You can't just turn up and hope for the best.

text.A2: You make your calls, asking the same thing each time. Can you help me get there? Send me the address. Give me a lift. Steady my nerves. Some say no — too busy, too far, bad timing. But a few say yes, and come through. Today, a few is enough.
text.B1: You make your calls, asking the same thing each time. Can you help me get there? Send me the address. Give me a lift. Steady my nerves. Some say no — too busy, too far, bad timing. But a few say yes, and come through for you. Today, a few is more than enough.
text.B2: You make your calls, asking the same thing each time. Can you help me get there? Send me the address. Give me a lift across town. Steady my nerves. Some say no — too busy, too far, bad timing all round. But a few say yes, and come through for you at once. Today, a few willing people is more than enough.

text.A2: You take charge of yourself and your papers. You lay it all out: your CV, the advert, your notes, the address. Done well, this is a real shot at the job. Rushed or half-done, and you walk in with nothing. So you take a breath and get it right, carefully.

text.B2: You take charge of yourself and your papers. You lay it all out neatly on the table: your CV, the printed advert, your notes, the address. So you take a slow breath and get it right, carefully, one thing at a time.

text.A2: You grab just the essentials — your CV and your phone — and go. It feels good to be moving at last. But it isn't a plan, and you've left things behind. You'll still need the rest, and soon. If not, you'll stand in that room with empty hands.

text.B2: You grab just the bare essentials — your CV and your phone — and go. It feels good to be moving at last, after all the panic. But it isn't a plan, and you've left real things behind. You'll still need the rest, and soon. If you don't go back for them, you'll be standing in that room with empty hands and nothing to show.

text.A2: Old Frank trained you years back, and he's seen it all. 'Don't cut the line to save time,' he says. 'It's not worth it — they always see.' He warns you about Reese too, the fixer. 'Walk in as yourself. Answer straight, stay calm. That's the whole job today.'
text.B1: Old Frank trained you years back, and he's seen it all in his time. 'Don't cut the line to save ten minutes,' he says. 'It's not worth it — they always see.' He warns you about Reese too, the fixer. 'Walk in as yourself. Answer straight, stay calm. That's the whole job today.'
text.B2: Old Frank trained you years back, and he's seen it all in his long time. 'Don't ever cut the line to save ten minutes,' he says. 'It's not worth it — they always see, in the end.' He warns you about Reese too, the fixer who works the station. 'Walk in as yourself. Answer straight, stay calm, and don't pretend. That's the whole job today.'

text.A2: You stop and help the stranger. He's an older man who's dropped his bag and papers all over the wet path. You gather them up and walk him to a dry seat. Little by little he calms down. 'Thank you,' he says, gripping your hand. You point him on his way, then turn back to the clock.

text.A2: Getting there comes first. The rest can wait a moment. But you still have to choose how. You could stop at the print shop for what you need first. Or you could set off now and sort the rest as you go.

text.A2: The rush catches up with you. Your hands shake, your heart races, and the clock won't stop. You're trying to do too much at once, and you know it. If you lose your head now, you'll lose the room. So slow down, breathe, one thing at a time.

text.A2: You call round, and people come through. One texts you the address. One offers a lift. One sends a kind word to steady your nerves. Bit by bit, you're not so alone. You still walk in by yourself. But now the getting-there isn't all on you — and that changes things.

text.A2: No one can help. One is at work, one is far away, one just doesn't pick up. You can't make them. So you square your shoulders and go on alone. It's harder this way. But the interview is at two, ready or not.

text.A2: You're on your way across the city. To reach the office in time, you have to cross town. There are two ways. The long way round is safe but slow. Cutting through and jumping the queue is quick. But it's risky, and people are watching.

text.A2: You take old Frank's words to heart. Walk in as yourself. Answer straight. Don't trust Reese. And don't cut any corners. It's simple advice, and good. Now you just have to follow it, with the clock running down.

text.A2: You feel better for the good turn you did. Helping someone, oddly, seems to steady you too. Your head is clearer, your hands are surer. There's still a lot to face before two. But now you feel able to meet it.

text.A2: In the waiting room, the other candidates sit stiff and silent. You break the ice — a small joke, a shared nerve. Slowly the room loosens up. 'You go next,' someone says, and you help each other get ready. It's a good feeling, with the clock running down.

text.A2: The long way is cold and wet, the rain on your face, no shelter at all. But it's safe, and it gets you there. So you keep walking, as fast as you dare, step after step. The clock ticks, but your feet keep moving.

text.A2: Jumping the queue up front would save you twenty minutes, and the platform is right there. But the guards are watching, the crowd is tight, and getting caught means losing it all. Frank told you not to cut the line. And he wasn't joking.

text.A2: You push into the front of the queue, past everyone waiting. At once it feels wrong. People glare and mutter, and a guard turns his head. Every step forward is a gamble now. And there's no going back once you've jumped the line.

text.B2: You help the young woman up and gather her scattered things. Her eyes fill with relief. She presses a small card into your hand — a name at the very firm you're headed to. 'Ask for her,' she says. 'Tell her I sent you.' A small thing — but freely given, in the rain, and you take it and go on your way.

text.A2: You can't stop now — but you can't just leave her, either. So you promise to send help soon. 'Hang on,' you say. 'Stay here, stay dry — someone will come.' You mean it, too. And then you turn and go.

text.B2: You can't stop now — but you can't simply leave her there, either. So you promise to send help soon. 'Hang on,' you say, over the rain. 'Stay here, stay dry — someone will come for you.' You mean it, too; and then you turn and go, carrying the weight of it with you.

text.A2: You get one good thing going — you help calm the whole waiting room at once. People breathe easier. Someone shares water, someone shares a laugh. It isn't the interview itself. But it's real, and it's a start.
text.B1: You get one good thing going — you help calm the whole waiting room at once. People breathe easier around you. Someone shares water, someone shares a laugh. It isn't the interview itself. But it's real, and it's a good start.
text.B2: You get one good thing going — you help calm the whole tense waiting room at once. People breathe easier around you now. Someone shares a bottle of water, someone shares a nervous laugh. It isn't the interview itself, not by a long way. But it's real, and it's a good start, and the room feels warmer for it.

text.A2: Person by person, the panic turns into a calm room. People have focus now: one reads notes, one breathes slow, one cheers the next in. Worry turns into doing. And doing beats worrying, every time. The room fills with a quiet, steady warmth.
text.B1: Person by person, the panic turns into a calm room. People have focus now: one reads notes, one breathes slow, one cheers the next one in. Worry turns into doing. And doing beats worrying, every single time. The room fills with a quiet, steady warmth.
text.B2: Person by person, nerve by nerve, the panic turns into a calm room. People have focus now: one reads over notes, one breathes slow, one quietly cheers the next one in. Worry turns into doing — and doing beats worrying, in a waiting room, every single time. The room fills with a quiet, steady warmth, and the worst of the fear lifts.

text.A2: The long morning wears at you. A voice says: give up, go home, tell them you were ill. No one would blame you, and it would be easy. But you think of your dad's face, and the room at two. And you push the voice away. Not yet.
text.B1: The long morning wears at you. A small voice says: give up, go home, tell them you were ill — no one would blame you, and it would be so easy. But you think of your dad's face, and the room at two. And you push the voice away. Not yet. Not while it can still go right.
text.B2: The long morning wears at you. A small voice says: give up, go home, tell them you were ill — no one would blame you, and it would be so easy to do. But you think of your dad's face, and the room waiting at two. And you push the voice away. Not yet. Not while this can still go right.

text.A2: You duck under a café awning to read your notes again. Half the ink has run in the rain. You could push on and trust what you remember. Or something makes you look up — and across the street, a face you half know.
text.B1: You duck under a café awning to read your notes again. Half the ink has run in the rain. You could push on and trust what you remember. Or something makes you look up — and there, across the street, a face you half know.
text.B2: You duck under a café awning to read your notes one more time. Half the ink has run and smudged in the rain. You could push on and trust what you remember. Or something makes you look up — and there, across the wet street, a face you half know, half dread.
